title: Proof pages for a developer-tool company
metaTitle: Proof pages for a developer-tool company
excerpt: Show the constraint, the decision, and a real screen of the tool. A gallery without a refused option is decoration. End by telling a similar engineer how to try it.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. The article is about editing proof down to a few pieces, the way a shop edits what it puts forward.
caption: A proof page should be edited like a small shop, not stocked like a warehouse. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes a developer-tool case study believable?
faqs.answer: Open on a constraint in the system, then on a decision that names the option you refused and what it cost. Show the real screen or transcript that embodies the choice. Engineers trust a cost and a refusal more than a tour of panels.

faqs.question: Should the page end on a sales form?
faqs.answer: End on how a similar reader can try the product, with one check that shows the try worked. Say when the decision would not transfer. Offer a conversation only as a second step, after the mechanism is in their hands.

faqs.question: Can you anonymize a customer story?
faqs.answer: You can omit the company name and still describe the kind of team and the kind of failure. Do not blend several customers into one hero. A labeled sample reconstruction is honest. A composite presented as a case is not.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A developer-tool company case study page should show a constraint, a decision, and a real screen of the tool. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing will ignore a gallery of interfaces. They want the limit you hit, the choice you made, and the artifact that choice produced. Then they want a way for a similar reader to try the product.

Screenshots without a decision are decoration. A tour of panels can prove that a design exists. It cannot prove that anyone refused a worse option. Refusal is the part this buyer trusts, because their own work is mostly refusal of bad defaults.

## Start from the constraint in the system

Open on the limit, not on the logo. A migration that locked a table. A test suite that cried wolf so often people stopped reading it. A trace that stopped at the framework and hid the query. Write the constraint as a behavior of a system, with the object named.

Say what it cost in engineering time. A class of incidents. A review bottleneck. A manual step before every release. Keep the cost in their week. Skip the language of pain points. It sounds like a form. The constraint should sound like a bug they have seen.

Include what had already been tried. A stricter lint. A bigger machine. A different vendor that solved a neighboring problem. The failed attempt keeps the story from pretending the team was naive. This reader is not naive. They will side with a story that respects that.

Leave the first screen free of a slogan. Nielsen Norman Group's summary of page-visit research is a fair editor. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds unless the page communicates its value immediately. On this page the value is the constraint. "A platform team needed to scale" communicates nothing. "The build passed while the migration locked production" communicates the next ten minutes.

You can anonymize the company. You should not anonymize the constraint into a platitude. Kind of team, kind of system, kind of failure. Specific and unnamed is still proof. Vague and branded is not.

## The decision, including the option you refused

Write one fork. You could have added a suppression comment and moved on. You refused, because the warning would vanish and the lock would remain. You failed the build instead, and you showed the offending statement. The fork should be visible in the tool afterward.

Name the trade. The build got noisier for a week. The incident got rarer. Or the tool got stricter and a class of users left, and you accepted that. A decision with no cost is a feature announcement. Put the cost in the paragraph. Engineers trust costs.

Say who chose. Their staff engineer. Your maintainer. A proof page that says the teams partnered to drive alignment has not chosen anything. Replace it with the fork and the names of the roles. You do not need a dramatic quote. You need the option that lost.

Google's people-first guidance favors first-hand experience over a recap that could have been written from a press release. If you were not close to the decision, talk to the person who was before you draft. If nobody can remember the refused option, you do not have a case. You have a release note. Publish the release note instead.

Keep one decision per page. A second fork can be a sentence if it served the same constraint. A pile of forks is a roadmap. The reader came to see judgment, not velocity.

## Show the real screen

After the decision, show the artifact. The comment on the pull request. The CLI output. The trace with the query visible. One frame, cropped to the line that matters. A sentence beside it should restate the choice. "The lock is named. The suppression we refused is not offered in this view."

Use the real UI. Blur secrets. Do not redraw the product to make the story prettier. This buyer is comparing your frame to tools they already run. A fantasy panel breaks the comparison and suggests the rest of the story was polished the same way.

A second frame can show the consequence. The build status. The quieter incident list. Two frames are a narrative. Six frames are a tour, and the decision dissolves. If you want a tour, publish a tour with a different title. Keep this page stern.

Say what did not change. Their language. Their CI vendor. The people on call. A case that claims a transformed engineering culture from one screen is the kind of page this reader has learned to mock. A changed default is enough, if the default mattered.

Place the words before the picture, or set them so the constraint is in the first screen even beside the image. A picture with no sentence is how galleries happen. The sentence is the proof. The picture is the exhibit.

If the tool's output is text, treat the text as the screen. A short transcript can be the exhibit. Indent it, keep the command accurate, and caption the line that embodies the decision. Do not restyle the output into a diagram that hides the actual words. Engineers trust a block they could have produced themselves. They distrust a polished panel that could only exist in a design file. When you have both a UI and a log, pick the one that shows the fork more clearly. The other can live in the docs as a reference, linked by its name, not pasted in to make the page feel longer.

## Why the gallery fails this reader

Equal screenshots assign equal importance. The hard line and the settings page become twins. The engineer cannot tell which one was the decision, so they assume there was no decision. They skim, confirm their skepticism, and install a competitor that showed the command.

A gallery also sneaks the slogan back in. Captions drift toward "a delightful review experience." Rewrite the caption as the fork, or remove the shot. If a frame cannot carry a refused option, it belongs in docs as a reference, not here as evidence.

Do not mix a logo wall into the story. Logos answer "who." This page answers "what was hard." A single line on the kind of team is plenty. The reader who needs brands can look elsewhere. The reader you want is checking the mechanism.

Motion tours and hotspots have the same problem when they cover the decision with interface tourism. Offer them in docs. On the proof page, a still and a sentence will be read. A tour will be abandoned by the same person who abandons a long README at the first badge row.

## End where a similar engineer can try

Close by naming the reader the story resembles. A team whose build is green while a migration is unsafe. A trace that stops too early. Invite them to try the product on that shape of problem. Tell them what to run. A sample migration. A repo they can throw away. The try path should match the homepage label so the site speaks one verb.

Say when the decision would not transfer. A different database. A monorepo size you have not seen. A language you do not parse. The fence is part of the proof. An engineer who sees it will try the product with the right expectation, or will correctly walk away. Both are better than a mismatched install.

Do not end on "contact sales" if the tool can be tried. The case was an argument for the mechanism. The ending should be the mechanism in their hands. A sales form at the bottom tells them the story was bait. If a conversation is useful after the trial, offer it as a second line, for the reader who reproduced the constraint and wants the paid fence.

Give them one thing to look for so they know the try worked. The warning names the statement. The trace shows the query. A checkable end is the opposite of a slogan.

## Publish only what you can defend

No invented metrics. No quotes you drafted. No timeline that compresses a quarter into a weekend unless that was the truth. If a number is sensitive, omit it. Describe the change in the system and stop. A missing percentage is not a hole. A fake one is a hole they will find.

Composites are fiction. If you need three customers to make one hero, you do not have a case yet. Wait. Publish a smaller true story. This audience has a long memory for amalgamations, and they share them.

Permission matters. If you cannot show the screen, rebuild the same situation in a sample and say that you did. A labeled reconstruction is honest. A stolen screenshot is not. Honesty is the point of a page aimed at skeptics.

Keep the page tight. One constraint. One decision. One real screen. A second theme means a second URL. Length is not depth. Depth is the refused option.

Once the page exists, the header has to make it findable under a word engineers already use. Read [how navigation should map jobs, including proof, without a department menu](/blog/navigation-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you file the story under a label called resources.

When you want the shape of a proof page checked against a real artifact, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the constraint and the screen. The gap between them is the draft.
